title: Das Märchen vom Schlauraffenland
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 158. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, that for tat).
about: KHM 158 is a tall-tale catalogue rather than a story with characters: it describes Schlauraffenland, the legendary land of Cockaigne where roast fowl fly, rivers run with honey, and every law of nature runs backward — a young donkey with a silver nose chases hares, mice consecrate a bishop, a snail outruns lions. There is no plot to follow; the pleasure is in the accumulating impossibilities, each stranger than the last, until a crowing hen calls the whole performance to a close.

sentences.t: In der Schlauraffenzeit da gieng ich, und sah an einem kleinen Seidenfaden hieng Rom und der Lateran,
sentences.l: In the Schlauraffen-time there I went, and saw on a small silk-thread hung Rome and the Lateran,
sentences.i: In the days of Schlauraffenland I went out, and saw Rome and the Lateran hanging from a little silken thread,
sentences.n: “Schlauraffenzeit” is the time of Schlauraffenland, the land of idleness and plenty where the roast birds fly into your mouth; the 1857 spelling keeps -au- where modern German writes Schlaraffenland. The “da” after the phrase is a spoken filler resuming it. The Lateran is the papal basilica in Rome: the tale hangs the whole church on a thread of silk.

sentences.t: und ein fußloser Mann der überlief ein schnelles Pferd und ein bitterscharfes Schwert das durchhieb eine Brücke.
sentences.l: and a footless man he outran a swift horse and a bitter-sharp sword it hewed through a bridge.
sentences.i: and a man with no feet outran a swift horse, and a bitingly sharp sword cut clean through a bridge.
sentences.n: Each item repeats its subject with a pronoun — “ein fußloser Mann der …” — the loose spoken syntax this whole tale is built out of. “überlief” and “durchhieb” take their prefixes inseparably, so the verbs stay in one piece where a separable verb would have thrown the particle to the end.

sentences.t: Da sah ich einen jungen Esel mit einer silbernen Nase, der jagte hinter zwei schnellen Hasen her,
sentences.l: Then I saw a young donkey with a silver nose, it chased behind two swift hares along,
sentences.i: Then I saw a young donkey with a silver nose, chasing after two swift hares,
sentences.n: “hinter … her jagen” = to chase after; the “her” at the end says the pursuit follows along behind. A donkey does not outpace hares, and there is nothing more to the item than that.

sentences.t: und eine Linde, die war breit, auf der wuchsen heiße Fladen.
sentences.l: and a linden, it was broad, on it grew hot flat-cakes.
sentences.i: and a linden tree, a broad one, with hot flat-cakes growing on it.
sentences.n: “heiße” here is the adjective heiß, ‘hot’ — not a form of heißen ‘to be called.’ “Fladen” are flat griddle-cakes; the impossibility is that they grow on the tree already hot.

sentences.t: Da sah ich eine alte dürre Geis, trug wohl hundert Fuder Schmalzes an ihrem Leibe und sechzig Fuder Salzes.
sentences.l: Then I saw an old lean nanny-goat, carried a good hundred cart-loads of lard on her body and sixty cart-loads of salt.
sentences.i: Then I saw an old scrawny nanny-goat carrying a good hundred cart-loads of lard on her body, and sixty of salt.
sentences.n: “Schmalzes” and “Salzes” are old genitives after a measure — cart-loads of lard, of salt — where modern German would leave the nouns unmarked. “wohl” is ‘a good, a full.’ A Fuder is as much as one cart will hold.

sentences.t: Ist das nicht gelogen genug?
sentences.l: Is that not lied enough?
sentences.i: Is that not lying enough for you?
sentences.n: The teller turns and asks the listener directly, once, in the middle of the catalogue and then never again. “gelogen” is the past participle of lügen, to tell an untruth, used here as a bare measure of the tale so far.

sentences.t: Da sah ich zackern einen Pflug ohne Roß und Rinder,
sentences.l: Then I saw a plough ploughing without horse and cattle,
sentences.i: Then I saw a plough tilling with neither horse nor oxen,
sentences.n: “zackern” is an old regional word for ploughing (modern ackern, pflügen); the infinitive stands before its subject, which the word order allows. A plough is drawn and never moves itself — that is the impossibility.

sentences.t: und ein jähriges Kind warf vier Mühlensteine von Regensburg bis nach Trier und von Trier hinein in Strasburg,
sentences.l: and a year-old child threw four millstones from Regensburg as far as Trier and from Trier right into Strasburg,
sentences.i: and a year-old child threw four millstones from Regensburg all the way to Trier, and from Trier into Strasburg,
sentences.n: “jährig” means a year old. The three towns are real and far apart — Regensburg on the Danube, Trier on the Moselle, Strasburg on the Rhine — which is what makes the throw absurd; “Strasburg” is the 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: und ein Habicht schwamm über den Rhein: das that er mit vollem Recht.
sentences.l: and a hawk swam across the Rhine: that he did with full right.
sentences.i: and a hawk swam across the Rhine — and did it by perfect right.
sentences.n: “Recht” here is the noun, right or law: “mit vollem Recht” = with every justification. The straight face is the joke — a hawk is entitled to swim if it chooses.

sentences.t: Da hört ich Fische mit einander Lärm anfangen, daß es in den Himmel hinauf scholl,
sentences.l: Then I heard fish start up a din with one another, so that it rang up into the sky,
sentences.n: “hört” is the plain past in its short form, ‘heard.’ “Lärm anfangen” is to start up a noise; “scholl” is the preterite of schallen, to resound. Fish are the proverbially silent creatures.

sentences.t: und ein süßer Honig floß wie Wasser von einem tiefen Thal auf einen hohen Berg;
sentences.l: and a sweet honey flowed like water from a deep valley onto a high mountain;
sentences.i: and sweet honey ran like water out of a deep valley up onto a high mountain;
sentences.n: “Thal” is the 1857 spelling of Tal. The impossibility here is the direction: the honey runs uphill.

sentences.t: das waren seltsame Geschichten.
sentences.l: those were strange stories.
sentences.i: those were strange doings.
sentences.n: “Geschichten” can mean stories told or goings-on that happen; here it sits closer to the second.

sentences.t: Da waren zwei Krähen, mähten eine Wiese, und ich sah zwei Mücken an einer Brücke bauen,
sentences.l: There were two crows, mowed a meadow, and I saw two gnats building at a bridge,
sentences.i: There were two crows mowing a meadow, and I saw two gnats at work building a bridge,
sentences.n: “Krähen” here is the plural noun, crows — not the verb krähen ‘to crow,’ which the tale keeps for its last line. “an etwas bauen” = to be at work building something. From here on everything comes in twos.

sentences.t: und zwei Tauben zerrupften einen Wolf, zwei Kinder die wurfen zwei Zicklein,
sentences.l: and two doves tore a wolf to pieces, two children they threw two kids,
sentences.i: and two doves plucked a wolf to pieces, two children dropped two goat-kids,
sentences.n: “wurfen” is an old preterite plural of werfen (modern warfen); of animals werfen means to give birth, so the children ‘throw’ two goat-kids in the sense of bearing them. Both senses of the verb are live in the line, and the tale does not settle which it means.

sentences.t: aber zwei Frösche droschen mit einander Getreid aus.
sentences.l: but two frogs threshed grain out with one another.
sentences.i: but two frogs threshed out grain together.
sentences.n: “droschen … aus” is ausdreschen, to thresh out, split around the rest of the clause. “Getreid” is the older form of Getreide.

sentences.t: Da sah ich zwei Mäuse einen Bischof weihen,
sentences.l: Then I saw two mice consecrate a bishop,
sentences.n: “weihen” is the church word for consecrating, and consecrating a bishop is an act only bishops may perform.

sentences.t: zwei Katzen, die einem Bären die Zunge auskratzten.
sentences.l: two cats, which scratched the tongue out of a bear.
sentences.i: and two cats that scratched a bear’s tongue out.
sentences.n: “einem Bären die Zunge” is the dative of possession again: the tongue belongs to the bear, so German says ‘to a bear the tongue’ rather than ‘the bear’s tongue.’

sentences.t: Da kam eine Schnecke gerannt und erschlug zwei wilde Löwen.
sentences.l: Then came a snail running and struck two wild lions dead.
sentences.i: Then a snail came running and struck two wild lions dead.
sentences.n: “kam … gerannt” — kommen with a past participle is the ordinary German way of saying how something arrived: came running. “erschlagen” is to kill by striking.

sentences.t: Da stand ein Bartscheerer, schor einer Frauen ihren Bart ab,
sentences.l: Then stood a beard-shearer, shaved a woman’s beard off her,
sentences.i: There stood a barber, shaving a woman’s beard off,
sentences.n: “Bartscheerer” is Bart ‘beard’ plus Scherer ‘shearer,’ the old word for a barber; the 1857 spelling doubles the e. “einer Frauen” is an old dative singular of Frau, and “ihren Bart” names the owner a second time — ‘to a woman her beard.’

sentences.t: und zwei säugende Kinder hießen ihre Mutter stillschweigen.
sentences.l: and two suckling children bade their mother be silent.
sentences.i: and two nursing babies told their mother to hold her tongue.
sentences.n: “heißen” with a bare infinitive means to bid or order someone to do a thing. “stillschweigen” = to keep silent.

sentences.t: Da sah ich zwei Windhunde, brachten eine Mühle aus dem Wasser getragen,
sentences.l: Then I saw two greyhounds, brought a mill carried out of the water,
sentences.i: Then I saw two greyhounds, carrying a mill up out of the water,
sentences.n: “brachten … getragen” pairs bringen with a past participle, the same construction as “kam gerannt” above: they brought it in a carrying manner. A watermill stands in the stream and does not leave it.

sentences.t: und eine alte Schindmähre stand dabei, die sprach es wäre Recht.
sentences.l: and an old broken-down nag stood by, it said it was right.
sentences.i: and an old broken-down nag stood by and said that it was right and proper.
sentences.n: “Schindmähre” is a worn-out horse fit only for the knacker — Schinder ‘flayer’ plus Mähre ‘mare.’ “wäre” is subjunctive, marking the nag’s words as reported. “Recht” is the noun again, as it was with the hawk.

sentences.t: Und im Hof standen vier Rosse, die droschen Korn aus allen Kräften,
sentences.l: And in the yard stood four steeds, they threshed grain with all their might,
sentences.i: And in the yard stood four steeds threshing grain with all their might,
sentences.n: “aus allen Kräften” = with all one’s strength. Horses tread out grain but never wield the flail; threshing is a man’s work.

sentences.t: und zwei Ziegen, die den Ofen heitzten, und eine rothe Kuh schoß das Brot in den Ofen.
sentences.l: and two goats, which heated the oven, and a red cow shot the bread into the oven.
sentences.i: and two goats that heated the oven, and a red cow that shot the bread into the oven.
sentences.n: “das Brot in den Ofen schießen” is the baker’s own phrase: the loaves are shot in on a long flat peel. “heitzten” and “rothe” are the 1857 spellings of heizten and rote.

sentences.t: Da krähte ein Huhn „kickeriki, das Märchen ist auserzählt, kickeriki.“
sentences.l: Then a hen crowed “kickeriki, the tale is told out, kickeriki.”
sentences.i: Then a hen crowed, “Cock-a-doodle-doo, the tale is told to the end, cock-a-doodle-doo.”
sentences.n: One last impossibility to close on: “ein Huhn” is a hen, and hens do not crow. “kickeriki” is the German cock’s cry. “auserzählt” is aus- ‘to the end’ plus erzählt ‘told.’

glossary.anfangen: anfangen — to begin, to start up (infinitive; „Lärm anfangen“ = to set up a din)
glossary.es: es — it (also the impersonal subject, as in „daß es … scholl“ = so that it rang)
glossary.frauen: die Frau — woman (old dat. sg. Frauen; also gen./pl.)
glossary.heiße: heiß — hot (adj., inflected); not a form of heißen ‘to be called’
glossary.hört: hören — heard (3rd/1st sg. past, short form; also hears)
glossary.krähen: die Krähe — crows (pl. Krähen); also krähen ‘to crow’
glossary.recht: das Recht — right, justice („mit vollem Recht“ = by full right); also the adverb recht ‘quite, properly’
glossary.rosse: das Roß — steeds (pl. Rosse; a higher word than Pferd)
glossary.roß: das Roß — steed, horse (1857 spelling of Ross; a higher word than Pferd)
